column4: One group explicitly counts its expenditure as a loss and waits for misfortune to strike the believers; the verse supplies the negative reckoning to which 9:99 gives the exact positive counterpart.
The person later described as showing off actively repels the orphan; this identifies whom his visible religion fails to serve.
He does not even urge the feeding of the poor; speech that could direct wealth to need is absent before the surah exposes show and withheld aid.
When relatives, orphans, and needy people attend a division of wealth, the command is both to provide for them and to speak kindly; hand and tongue jointly serve real recipients.
The sacrificial animals’ flesh and blood do not reach God, but mindfulness does; visible quantity and material transfer are expressly distinguished from what makes the act count with God.
The defrauders demand full measure when receiving from people; their calculation magnifies what comes to themselves.
When measuring or weighing for others, they diminish it; the paired verses expose a self-serving ledger that counts incoming and outgoing goods by different standards.
The rivalry in increase continues until people visit the graves; death supplies the limit that the quantity contest in 102:1 suppresses.
Secret conversation has value when it directs charity or reconciliation and seeks God’s pleasure; social speech becomes a means of giving rather than self-advertisement.
The Messenger is told to take charity that purifies its owners and to pray for them; purification and divinely authorized reassurance replace praise solicited from spectators.
Those seeking their Lord’s face spend from His provision secretly and openly; the same two visibility modes are governed by a single nonhuman audience.
Sacrificial camels are named among God’s signs, and people are told to eat from them and feed both the reticent and the petitioner; herd-wealth visibly becomes food for actual mouths.
Solomon asks whether the envoys would supply him with wealth and says what God gave him is better; he refuses to let a displayed gift determine his rank.
He returns the gift and warns its senders, rejecting the attempt to purchase favor or reputation through wealth.
Those who leave their beds to call on their Lord also spend from what He provided; hidden devotion and expenditure are joined without a human audience.
No soul knows the hidden delight reserved as recompense for their deeds; the reward is kept outside the public field in which praise is sought.
People are told to spend from that over which God made them successors; delegated possession undercuts the claim that consumed wealth was autonomously one’s own.
A good loan to God is multiplied and receives a noble reward; divine accounting turns apparent depletion into increase.
Charitable men and women who make a good loan to God have it multiplied; the repeated promise makes the lasting return depend on the recipient of the act, not spectators.
The distribution rule prevents wealth from circulating only among the rich and assigns it to named communities; destination, rather than a donor’s quantity, governs the social account.
Whatever good people send ahead they will find with God as something better and greater in reward; the true ledger preserves what leaves the hand.
The giver who seeks only his Lord’s face will finally be satisfied; this completes 92:18–20 with a return received from God rather than from human thanks.
God says He raised the Prophet’s remembrance; elevated public mention is bestowed by God rather than manufactured through a boast.

Givers must spend from the good things they earned and may not select inferior goods they themselves would accept only reluctantly; the quality of what reaches another person matters alongside amount.
Satan threatens poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty; the fear of depletion behind withholding is set against the divine account developed through this spending passage.
The wealth and children of disbelievers will not avail them against God; possessed abundance cannot provide the power its owner imagines.
The same formula recurs: neither wealth nor children will avail their owners against God, making worldly means fail at the decisive audience.
Earlier peoples were stronger and had more wealth and children, yet their deeds became void; greater quantities and worldly enjoyment do not survive the account.
Moses identifies Pharaoh’s adornment and wealth as means of misguidance and asks that the wealth be obliterated; displayed riches and their destructive end are specifically joined.
The deeds of disbelievers are like ashes scattered by wind, and they can retain nothing of what they earned; this images the nullity included in the section’s destruction-root.
Squanderers are called brothers of devils; the verse supplies the moral judgment between the command to give rightful dues and the measured hand of 17:29.
Humans would withhold even God’s inexhaustible treasuries for fear of spending them away; the imagined exhaustion of wealth is exposed as a motive for possessiveness.
When revelations are recited, disbelievers ask which party has the better station and finer assembly; public appearance and social company are made into an argument for rank.
God answers that He destroyed generations superior in possessions and outward appearance; the reputation comparison in 19:73 ends in divine destruction.
A disbeliever’s deeds are like a mirage he supposes to be water until he finds God, who pays his account in full; false visual appraisal gives way to the real reckoning.
On the decisive day neither wealth nor children benefit; the assets used to establish rank have no purchasing power in the final scene.
Whatever people are given is worldly enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and more lasting; visible possession is explicitly set against duration.
Past peoples were more numerous, stronger, and greater in visible آثار, yet what they earned did not avail them; repeated social superiority ends in repeated failure.
When messengers came, those peoples rejoiced in the knowledge they possessed; the self-crediting claim associated with Qarun reappears as their spoken ground of confidence.

The condemned are told that they exhausted their good things in worldly life and enjoyed them, then receive humiliation for arrogance; present consumption and public pride leave no favorable remainder.
Neither wealth nor children avail their owners against God; the repeated boundary denies worldly means any protective force at the account.
The hypocrites say not to spend on those with the Messenger so that they disperse, although God owns the treasuries; speech directs withheld wealth toward social control rather than need.
The garden owners are introduced as a test when they swear to harvest in the morning; their property becomes the site where confident planning and exclusion will be judged.
They make no exception; whether heard as failing to qualify their plan or to reserve a share, the wording marks the closed certainty behind their intended exclusion.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while they sleep; destruction occurs outside the owners’ sight despite their confidence in controlling the harvest.
By morning the garden is like a dark, stripped field; the wealth meant to be withheld has itself been removed.
The most balanced among them recalls having told the others to glorify God; proper speech would have acknowledged the Giver before the boast of control hardened.
They finally glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing; the owners’ later words replace confident possession with accountable self-recognition.
God recalls giving the opponent extensive wealth; the wealth behind his demand for more is provision received, not a self-created badge.
Despite extensive wealth and social support, he still covets increase; abundance feeds the count instead of satisfying it.
The warning to defrauders introduces a commercial scene in which quantities are deliberately made to serve the self.
The defrauders do not suppose they will be resurrected; crooked earthly measurement is sustained by a false estimate of the coming account.
Their resurrection is for a tremendous day, giving the self-serving transaction its larger horizon.
On that day humanity stands before the Lord of all worlds; the people whose measures favored themselves face the one impartial audience.
The graves being overturned establishes the final exposure in which the hidden contents of hearts are brought out in 100:10.
After wealth and earnings fail to avail in 111:2, the owner enters a blazing fire; the possessed means end in liability rather than rescue.
